newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel sees tax compromise despite talks collapse.
newsitem.headline: Waigel sees tax compromise despite talks collapse.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Sunday he believed a compromise with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on the thorny issue of tax reform was still possible despite the collapse of talks last week.

Waigel said in an interview with the newspaper Bild am Sonntag that there was scope for agreement on the centre-right coalition government's proposals for a bottom tax rate of a 15 percent, and for a peak rate of 35 percent on corporate tax.

"A sensible peak rate for private income follows almost automatically from that," Waigel said, adding that he still saw January 1 1999 as a "realistic starting date" for the introduction of the tax reform plan.

The government needs SPD cooperation to pass Waigel's bill to complete 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion) in tax cuts, since the SPD has the power to block most of the measures with its majority in the Upper House of parliament.
SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine accused the government of trying to conceal from voters a "vast tax increase programme" from 1999 onwards to cover a revenue shortfall of 60 billion marks.

Talks between the two sides aimed at securing a consensus collapsed in acrimony last Wednesday, consigning the tax measures to a tortuous passage through parliament and a likely deadlock in a parliamentary arbitration panel.
Since then both sides have engaged in a war of words, with each blaming the other for barring action to put Germany's 4.5 million unemployed back to work.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Friday that the SPD could not block tax reform indefinitely.

"Tax reform is coming. There is no doubt of that," he said in the Frankfurt Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung. Waigel said there was scope for compromise on government proposals, vehemently opposed by the SPD, to cut tax breaks on shift and night-time work.
Lafontaine accused the government of delaying its tax reform until 1999 to hide planned tax increases.
"Kohl's government is planning a drastic increase in value added tax and petrol tax to finance its tax reform," Lafontaine told the daily Suedkurier on Saturday.

Lafontaine repeated his allegation that Waigel would have to cover a shortfall of 56 billion marks for 1999 under current tax forecasts, and that this would grow beyond 60 billion when tax revenue estimates are released next month.
He said Waigel planned to add 20 pfennigs -- around 12 percent -- to the price of a litre of petrol and raise value added tax by two points to 17 percent.

Waigel has also not ruled out a spending freeze, tax hikes or a cut in welfare benefits to cut the budget deficit below the Maastricht treaty limit of three percent of GDP this year to ensure Germany joins the European monetary union starting lineup in 1999.
In the talks which collapsed last week, the two sides come close to agreeing to cut the bottom rate of income tax and reduce corporation tax.
The main sticking point was Waigel's plan to cut the top rate of income tax to 39 percent in 1999 from 53 percent.
The SPD also fundamentally opposed the government's supply-side approach to encourage corporate investment.
The SPD demanded above all that a big cut in non-wage labour costs -- unemployment, health and pensions insurance charges -- be made this year to boost consumer demand. ($ = 1.727 German Marks)
